food.text: Aboriginal Australians lived on native foods, known as bush tucker, throughout the medieval centuries. Animal foods included kangaroo, emu and witchetty grubs, while plant foods included fruits such as quandong and vegetables such as warrigal greens and various native yams.

Aboriginal Australians divided the work of feeding a group. Males generally hunted large game, while females gathered local staples such as small animals, shellfish, vegetables, fruits, seeds and nuts. Food was shared within groups and exchanged across groups.
An estimated 4,999 species of native food were used by Aboriginal peoples. Much of it was unsafe or unpalatable raw, so it had to be processed before eating.

Aboriginal cooks processed food by cooking it on open fires, boiling it in bark containers, pounding vegetables and seeds, or hanging bags in running water. Toxic seeds, such as Cycas media and Moreton Bay chestnut, were processed to remove the toxins and render them safe to eat. Some animals, such as kangaroos, were cooked in their own skins, and others, such as turtles, in their own shells.
Fire-stick farming, in use in many parts of Australia since 46,000 years ago, cleared vegetation and made travel easier. It also created open grasslands rich in animal and vegetable food sources.

Australian native plant foods include the fruits quandong, kutjera, muntries and riberry, and spices such as lemon myrtle and mountain pepper. Nuts include the bunya nut and the macadamia nut, the best-known bush tucker plant harvested and sold in large commercial quantities today.

Some Aboriginal groups engaged in fire-stick farming, fish farming, and built semi-permanent shelters. How far some groups practised agriculture is controversial, and some anthropologists describe traditional Aboriginal Australia as a complex hunter-gatherer society.
In the Torres Strait, agriculture developed on some islands, and by about 700 years ago villages had appeared. The Torres Strait Islanders also had a distinctive maritime culture.
Aboriginal Australians used the stars as a food calendar. The Boorong people of Victoria know that when the Malleefowl (Lyra) disappears in October, it is time to start gathering her eggs on Earth.

Some Aboriginal groups read the sky for signs about food. They know that when Orion first appears, the dingo puppies are about to be born, and that heliacal risings and settings tell them when to move to a new place or look for a new food source.

Knowledge of Aboriginal uses of fungi is meagre, but beefsteak fungus and native bread, which is also a fungus, were certainly eaten. They are a small part of the wide range of foods gathered from the land.

art.text: The oldest known canoe remains found in New Zealand were uncovered near the Anaweka estuary in the Tasman District. Radiocarbon dating placed the vessel at about 1400, making it one of the earliest known examples of Māori watercraft construction in the region.

By around 1500, as Māori society entered what is known as the Classic period, an increasing population, competition for resources and a cooling climate drove social and cultural change. Sudden cooling from about 1500 came with massive earthquakes on the South Island Alpine fault, a major earthquake around 1460 near Wellington, tsunamis that destroyed many coastal settlements, and the extinction of the moa and other food species. A more elaborate art form developed, with finely made pounamu (greenstone) weapons and ornaments and elaborately carved canoes, alongside a fierce warrior culture of fortified hillforts known as pā. The Classic Māori also practised cannibalism and built some of the largest war canoes (waka taua) ever made.

The didgeridoo was developed by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia at least 1,000 years ago. It is a wind instrument played with vibrating lips and a breathing technique called circular breathing, which produces a continuous drone. In the Yolŋu languages of northeast Arnhem Land it is called the yiḏaki.

Tā moko is the permanent marking or tattooing practised by Māori, one of the five main Polynesian tattoo styles. In pre-European Māori culture, many if not most high-ranking people received moko. It was associated with mana and high social status.

Māori visual art consists mainly of four forms: carving (whakairo), tattooing (tā moko), weaving (raranga) and painting (kōwhaiwhai). It was rare for any of them to be purely decorative. Traditional Māori art was highly spiritual and, in an oral society, carried knowledge and ancestry.
The Anaweka canoe was built in New Zealand and was a sophisticated craft. Its design was compatible with the style of other Polynesian voyaging canoes of that time, around 1400.

Traditionally, the didgeridoo accompanied ceremonial dancing and singing. For the Yolngu people, the yidaki is tied to their Law and underpinned by ceremony, in song, dance, visual art and stories. It is part of their whole physical and cultural landscape.

The Moriori settled the Chatham Islands from mainland New Zealand by at least about 1500, and possibly around the mid-15th century. Their culture diverged from mainland Māori, and they developed a distinct language, mythology and artistic expression of their own.

Archaeological studies that date rock art in the Kakadu region suggest the didgeridoo has been used there for less than 1,000 years. A clear painting at Ginga Wardelirrhmeng, on the northern edge of the Arnhem Land plateau, shows a didgeridoo player and two song-men taking part in an Ubarr ceremony.

Tattooists, called tohunga-tā-moko, were considered tapu, meaning inviolable and sacred. Some very high-status individuals were thought too tapu to receive moko themselves. Historically the skin was carved with uhi, chisels made from albatross bone, hafted onto a handle and struck with a mallet. This left the skin with grooves rather than a smooth surface, and a kōrere, or feeding funnel, is believed to have been used to feed men whose mouths had become swollen from receiving tā moko.

Across Moana Oceania, creative hubs of knowledge called whare wānanga trained specialists, known as tohunga, including arts specialists. Artistic skills were valued by Māori, and leaders were expected to show skill in the arts. A specific design on an object could invoke a god, or atua, and make the item more effective.

A 6 cm-long Polynesian pearl fishing-lure was found at Tairua in 1962 and reliably dated to the early to mid-14th century. It was found at a small coastal moa-hunters' site, and it links the early settlers of New Zealand to the craft traditions of Polynesia.

At Wairau Bar, a turret shell found only in the South Pacific islands, most notably the Society Islands, had been reworked into a small chisel. It was dated to about 1300. The shell is one of two artefacts that link early settlers in New Zealand to Polynesia.

war.text: The Classic period saw a new warrior culture emerge among Māori, with fortified villages known as pā, alongside a more elaborate art form. The article calls it a fierce warrior culture that built hillforts known as pā, practised cannibalism, and made some of the largest war canoes (waka taua) ever built. It followed a cooling climate from about 1500, massive earthquakes, tsunamis that destroyed many coastal settlements, and the extinction of the moa and other food species.

During the early 'Archaic' period of Māori settlement, communities notably lacked the weapons and fortifications that later became typical of 'Classic' Māori culture. This phase lasted from the time of the first settlers' arrival until about 1500.

More than 5,000 pā, fortified hilltop villages defended with palisades and terraces, have been found mainly in New Zealand's North Island. This tradition of Māori fortification-building traces back around 500 years.

The Moriori migrated from mainland New Zealand to the Chatham Islands, possibly around the mid-15th century. As a small and precarious population, they embraced a pacifist culture that rigidly avoided warfare, banned it along with cannibalism, and replaced it with ritual fighting. Men could strike each other only with a rod the thickness of a thumb, and at the first sign of blood honour was to be considered satisfied. Moriori also castrated some male infants in order to control population growth.

The best-studied site from this early period is Wairau Bar, in New Zealand's South Island. It was occupied from the early 13th century to the early 15th century, a time when Māori settlements show little evidence of the weaponry seen in later history.
A great pā stood for the mana, or prestige and power, of the iwi that built it. It was personified by its rangatira, or chieftain, and showcased the tribe's strategic strength.
Great pā included a community well for water and designated waste areas. An elevated lookout held a wooden alarm block called a pahū, which would be struck to warn residents of an attack.

Some researchers guess that the Moriori's ancestors arrived not in a war canoe but a trading canoe, since women must have been on board. It was likely blown off course while traveling from the far south, sometime between 1400 and 1500.

Moriori avoided warfare in order to conserve resources, but the lack of training in warfare led to their near-destruction. In 1835 Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama Māori invaded the Chatham Islands with guns, clubs and axes. A Moriori survivor recalled that the invaders began to kill them like sheep, men, women and children indiscriminately. Some 10% of the population were ritually killed, and stakes were driven into some of the women, who were left to die in pain. The survivors were enslaved, and only 101 Moriori out of about 2,000 were left alive by 1862.

literature.text: According to Māori history, Kupe was the first person to discover New Zealand, arriving with his wife Kuramārōtini on the canoe Matahourua. Most histories place the voyage between 900 and 1200 AD. On the way home, according to oral history, Kupe sacrificed his son Tuputupu-whenua at Hokianga Harbour, drowning him in the spring of Te Puna-o-te-ao-Mārama to guard the land from under the water while he was gone.

Māori oral histories recount how ancestors sailed to New Zealand from a homeland called Hawaiki aboard ocean-going canoes known as waka. Some tribal stories say these migrations were made to escape famine, over-population and warfare, in legendary canoes such as Aotea, Te Arawa, Kurahaupō, Mātaatua, Tainui, Tākitimu and Tokomaru. In the story of Kupe, he murdered Hoturapa, owner of the great canoe Matahourua, eloped with Hoturapa's wife Kūrāmarotini, and fled in the canoe to escape punishment, then discovered Aotearoa.

Aboriginal Australians recorded their history and geography in songlines, oral song cycles that mark the routes travelled by ancestral creator-beings across the land. By singing these songs in the correct order, people could navigate vast distances, including one route said to stretch 3,500 kilometres from the Central Desert Region to Byron Bay on the east coast.

Whakapapa, meaning genealogy or 'layering,' was a fundamental form of Māori oral literature that let people recite their lineage across many generations. Reciting one's whakapapa proclaimed identity and linked a person to land and tribal groupings, and experts could trace connections in both a linear and lateral sense.

According to Māori tradition passed down orally, haka originated from a creation story about the sun god Tama-nui-te-rā and his two wives, the Summer Maid Hine-raumati and the Winter Maid Hine-takurua. Haka was said to begin with the shimmering haze of Hine-raumati's presence, personified as Tāne-rore, her son with Tama-nui-te-rā.

Oral traditions describe Kupe's voyage and settlement of New Zealand occurring around 1000 to 1300 CE, retelling his hunting and destruction of the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi. These stories differ between Māori iwi, since each group preserved its own version orally.

In the 'Great Fleet' account by the 19th-century ethnologist Percy Smith, seven canoes left the Tahitian region together in 1350 CE, carrying advanced, warlike, agricultural tribes who destroyed the Moriori, a supposed primitive pre-Māori people. This story was taught in New Zealand schools until ethnologist David Simmons showed in the 1960s that it came from an incomplete, indiscriminate reading of 19th-century traditions. The Moriori are now understood to be an isolated offshoot of Māori who settled the Chatham Islands around 1500 CE. The historian Rawiri Taonui accuses Smith of falsification, saying he 'cut and pasted' separate oral traditions into new ones.

The Dreaming describes an 'Everywhen' in which ancestral figures, often of heroic or supernatural stature, created and shaped the land. Certain locations held a distinct potency within this tradition, including Uluru, also known as Ayers Rock, and Kata Tjuta, also called Mt. Olga.

Māori oral literature took three main forms: genealogical recital, poetry, and narrative prose, all preserved by experts called tohunga. Because Māori had no writing system before European contact began in 1769, these traditions, inherited from the Polynesian homeland Hawaiki, were memorised and retold from generation to generation.

Māori narrative tradition tells of Māui, a demigod and trickster, who was credited with catching a giant fish that became New Zealand's North Island, known as Te Ika-a-Māui. His brothers would not lend him any bait, so he struck himself on the nose and baited a hook made from his grandmother's jawbone with his own blood. When the fish was hauled up, his brothers began to cut it up before the proper ceremonies could be done, and the fish writhed in agony, breaking into mountains, cliffs and valleys. In some traditions, his canoe became the South Island, known as Te Waka a Māui.

Reciting whakapapa within Māori oral tradition served as a kind of timescale linking the distant past to the present, connecting living people to gods and legendary heroes. A narrator who quoted the correct genealogical lines thereby proved their right to speak of the characters and deeds being described.

The haka called Ka Mate, still performed today, was composed by Te Rauparaha of Ngāti Toa to commemorate his escape from death in 1810, when, chased by his enemies, he hid in a food-storage pit under the skirt of a woman. The story was merely woven into several older oral traditions, including a rope-hauling chant used to beach a 14th-century voyaging waka and a call for unity under one strong leader. At the end it took in an erotic wedding-night chant called 'Kikiki Kakaka.'

science.text: Moa were giant flightless birds unique to New Zealand, with the largest species reaching about 3.6 metres in height and 230 kilograms in weight. After Māori settlers arrived around 1300 CE, moa were hunted until none were left. Their extinction came within 100 years of human settlement, primarily because of overhunting, and every species was gone by 1445 CE.

Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometres of open Pacific Ocean using wayfinding techniques based on the stars, ocean swells, wind patterns and the behaviour of birds. This oral tradition of navigation let Polynesian voyagers reach New Zealand and other outlying islands of the South Pacific by 1500.

Australian Aboriginal peoples built up detailed astronomical knowledge, passed down through oral tradition, ceremony and artwork, tracking the rising and setting of stars and constellations. The Boorong people, for example, treated the disappearance of the Malleefowl constellation in October as the sign to start gathering the bird's eggs, showing how the stars guided seasonal food gathering.

The Maramataka is a Māori lunar calendar of twelve months, used to time activities such as fishing, eeling and planting according to the phases of the moon. It was a practical tool passed down to help communities know when to gather particular foods throughout the year.

The oldest known Māori canoe remains were found near the Anaweka estuary in the Tasman District and have been radiocarbon-dated to about 1400. The vessel was built in New Zealand yet matched the sophisticated style of other Polynesian voyaging canoes of that period.

Physical evidence of Polynesian voyaging into what is called 'South Polynesia' includes a canoe found on Chatham Island dated to between 1440 and 1470, and settlement remains on Enderby Island in the Auckland Islands dated back to the 13th century. These finds show Polynesian navigators travelling far beyond New Zealand's main islands using their wayfinding skills.

The upland moa lived in the alpine and subalpine regions of New Zealand's South Island, feeding on flowers, herbs and other vegetation at elevations up to 2000 metres. When the Māori arrived from Polynesia around AD 1250 to 1300, they found the docile moa an easy source of food. The birds were hunted to extinction, and the upland moa, the last known surviving moa species, was gone by AD 1445.

A partial egg found at the Rakaia River, tentatively attributed to the upland moa, has been radiocarbon-dated to roughly AD 1300 to AD 1400. Unusually, its shell was dark olive green rather than white, making the upland moa likely the only moa species known to lay eggs that were not white.

Estimates of how many moa lived in New Zealand around the time Polynesians settled circa 1300 CE vary enormously, ranging from as few as 58,000 to as many as 2.5 million birds. This huge range reflects how uncertain scientists remain about moa numbers before the birds were driven to extinction.

Māori tradition holds that the Arawa voyaging canoe was shaped using two adzes, one called Tūtauru and made from New Zealand greenstone that the explorer Ngāhue had brought back. Another great canoe, Tainui, was built from a tree felled at the same place and time using the same methods.

The Maramataka's twelve months normally run in sequence, but the two months following the harvest month of Poutū-te-rangi are traditionally treated as quiet periods with little activity. Because so little happens during these two months, they are sometimes customarily removed from the calendar altogether.

politics.text: According to Māori oral tradition, ancestors arrived in New Zealand from Polynesia around 1350 in a series of planned ocean-going canoe voyages. These voyagers became the founders of New Zealand's tribal Māori communities, developing over the following centuries their own distinct culture separate from other Polynesian societies.

According to Tainui historian Pei Te Hurinui Jones, the Tainui people first entered New Zealand's Waikato region around the year 1400. They brought kumara plants with them, introducing this crop to the area.

The Moriori people settled the remote Chatham Islands by at least about 1500 AD, possibly arriving as early as the mid-15th century. In 2019 the researcher Richards proposed that the first settlers likely arrived from mainland New Zealand around 1450.

Fortified Māori villages called pā, which displayed a tribe's mana, or prestige, and its strategic strength, are known to have existed for around 500 years. Their rise coincided with growing iwi rivalry over resources and territory, which began to bring about greater warfare.

These Polynesian settlers organized themselves into iwi, or tribes, tracing their ancestry back to the homeland of Hawaiki. Each iwi was in turn made up of smaller hapū, or subtribes, and whānau, or extended family groups.

The early Moriori who settled the Chatham Islands organized themselves into tribal groups based on eastern Polynesian social customs. Over time their culture diverged from that of mainland Māori, developing its own distinct language, mythology and way of life.

Each hapū's rangatira, or chief, was often a hereditary leader who held mana, or authority, on behalf of the tribe. Part of a rangatira's role was maintaining the rohe, the boundary separating one tribe's land from that of its neighbors.
Each hapū, or subtribe, functioned as the basic political unit within Māori society. It was traditionally led by its own chief and normally operated independently of the wider iwi it belonged to.

A Moriori oceangoing waka discovered on the northern coast of Chatham Island in 2024 has been dated to between about 1440 and 1470. This places it right around the time the islands were first settled by voyagers from mainland New Zealand.

In October 2014, the remains of a canoe called the Papanui waka were found in the sand dunes of Papanui Inlet. Dated to the 15th century, it likely came from the time the Waitaha iwi occupied the area, making it the second oldest known waka in New Zealand.

culture.text: Māori are descended from East Polynesian settlers who arrived in New Zealand in several waves of canoe voyages, mainly between about 1320 and 1350. Over the following centuries in isolation, they developed a distinct culture, with language, mythology, crafts and performing arts that evolved independently from other Polynesian cultures.

Moa were giant flightless birds found only in New Zealand, with the largest species standing about 3.6 metres tall with neck outstretched and weighing around 230 kilograms. Polynesians settling New Zealand around 1300 CE encountered moa populations that may have numbered as many as 2.5 million birds.

Māori built pā, fortified villages with palisades and terraces, mostly in the North Island of New Zealand, and over 5,000 such sites have since been located. A great pā represented the mana, or prestige, and strategic skill of an iwi, led by a chief called a rangatira.

Māori practised tā moko, permanent tattooing applied by tattooists known as tohunga-tā-moko, who were considered tapu, or sacred. Historically the skin was carved with chisels rather than punctured with needles, leaving it grooved. Men generally received moko on their faces, buttocks and thighs, while women usually wore moko on their lips and chins.

In traditional Māori religion, practised before European contact, everything, including natural elements and all living things, was seen as connected through whakapapa, or genealogy. Māori believed that all things possessed a life force called mauri.

Māori built waka, from small unornamented canoes used for fishing and river travel to large carved war canoes called waka taua, up to 40 metres long and manned by as many as 80 paddlers. Māori told missionaries during the Musket Wars that waka fought at sea by ramming an enemy's waka amidships at high speed, riding up over its gunwale to force it under water or roll it over. This matches the 1642 attack on Abel Tasman's ship's boat in Golden Bay, when a Māori catamaran rammed a cockboat and four Dutch sailors were killed. The oldest known Māori-built canoe remains, found near the Anaweka estuary, have been radiocarbon-dated to about 1400.

The earliest period of Māori settlement, called the Archaic or Moahunter period, ran from first arrival to about 1500. Early Māori ate large amounts of moa and other large birds, along with fur seals, none of which had ever been hunted before. The moa and other food species later went extinct, which helped bring the Archaic period to an end. The era is known for its distinctive reel necklaces and for a lack of weapons and fortifications.

Before humans arrived, the moa's only predator was the giant Haast's eagle, which relied on moa for food. New Zealand had few predators, so its native species were ill-equipped to cope with human predators. After Polynesians settled around 1300 CE, all moa genera were soon driven to extinction by hunting and, to a lesser extent, forest clearance. By 1445 CE all moa were extinct, and Haast's eagle, which had relied on them for food, became extinct along with them.

Inside a pā, a community well supplied water and storage pits kept crops such as kūmara safe. An alarm called a pahū, a grooved piece of wood struck to sound a warning, stood on a raised outpost, while the chief's whare on the summit could measure 4.5 by 4 metres.

Receiving moko marked an important passage from childhood to adulthood and was accompanied by many rites and rituals. Moko signalled a person's mana and high social status, though some very high-status individuals were considered too tapu to receive it.

In Māori society before European contact, tapu was one of the strongest forces in Māori life. A violation of tapu could have dire consequences, including the death of the offender through sickness or at the hands of someone affected by the offence. Food cooked for a person of high rank was tapu and could not be eaten by an inferior, and a chief's house was tapu, as were the possessions of people of high rank, including their clothing. A person of lower rank who touched the belongings of a highborn person put themselves at risk of death.

Radiocarbon dating shows Polynesian voyagers reached outlying islands south of New Zealand, known as 'South Polynesia', by 1500. The remains of an oceangoing waka found on Chatham Island have been dated to between 1440 and 1470, showing voyaging into the region during this era.
